subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Feynman Technique
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Feynman Technique.

hook.text: Richard Feynman said if you can't explain something simply, you don't truly understand it.

buildup.text: His technique: study, then explain it as if teaching a child. Where you stumble, you have gaps.

discovery.text: Teaching forces you to organize, simplify, and connect ideas. It exposes hidden confusion.

twist.text: The "protégé effect" confirms it: students who teach material score higher than those who just study.

climax.text: Even pretending to teach—explaining to an empty room—activates deeper processing in the brain.

quiz.question: Why is teaching material effective for learning?
options: It forces organization and exposes gaps

details.summary: The Feynman technique involves explaining a concept in simple terms as if teaching it to someone with no background. When you struggle to explain clearly, you have found a gap in your understanding. The process of simplifying forces deep processing and exposes superficial knowledge.
details.whyItMatters: The Feynman technique operationalizes deep learning. If you cannot explain it simply, you do not understand it well enough. Teaching forces the deepest level of processing.
takeaways: Explain concepts in the simplest possible terms
Gaps in your explanation reveal gaps in understanding
Teaching forces deeper processing than passive review

faq.question: How do you use the Feynman technique step by step?
faq.answer: Choose a concept and write it at the top of a page. Explain it in simple language as if teaching a child. When you get stuck or use jargon, go back to the source material and fill the gap. Simplify and use analogies. Repeat until the explanation flows clearly without technical crutches.

faq.question: Why is teaching such an effective way to learn?
faq.answer: Teaching requires you to organize, simplify, and connect information, which forces deep processing. You must anticipate questions and fill gaps. Research on the protege effect shows that students who teach material to others learn it better than those who study for a personal test.
